title: A page, or less
hookLine: Daf Yomi, or a slower pace; both count
tomorrow: can you pray in a language you barely read?

lines: A SCRAPE, THEN A SMALL SLAP.
DAF: A PAGE, FRONT AND BACK.
cards: Listen to a page turn: a soft scrape, then a small slap as it lands. The Hebrew word daf means a page, a leaf, with a front and a back. Daf Yomi is a page of Talmud a day, the same page for everyone who keeps it.
It sounds heroic. And if a page a day would break you? The tradition's answer about half a page is gentler than you might expect.

teach.h: NOT YOURS TO FINISH. DON'T QUIT.
teach.b: Start with Rabbi Tarfon, in Pirkei Avot: it isn't on you to finish the work, but you aren't free to walk away from it either. Both halves matter. Not finishing is allowed.
Stopping is the thing to avoid.
Then a line from Proverbs, read by the Talmud as advice for learners: whoever gathers little by little will have more.
The Talmud explains: someone who crams learning in big bundles ends up with less, and someone who gathers a little at a time ends up with more.

teach.h: THE RABBIS KNOW, AND CRAM ANYWAY.
teach.b: Then it adds, almost laughing at itself, that the rabbis know this, and don't do it. So a page a day is one pace. Half a page is a pace.
One line, read every morning before you check your phone, is a pace.

teach.h: A SET TIME, NOT A SET SIZE.
teach.b: Shammai's advice in Pirkei Avot is to make your study fixed: a set time, not a set size.
What counts is coming back. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud admits the sages knew slow and steady works, and crammed anyway.

how: Some Jews study a daf, a page of Talmud, every day on the shared Daf Yomi schedule; others keep a slower fixed time, a few lines or a half page, alone or with a partner.

a lesson a teacher gives each week
one leaf of Talmud, front and back

games.q: your mom wants to study but has only ten minutes on the train each morning. she says: what's the point, it's barely anything. what fits today's teaching?
o: a fixed ten minutes counts; little by little, it grows.
wait for a week off, then study it all in one big push.
skip it; less than a page a day doesn't really count.
games.why: the Talmud says learning gathered little by little increases, and Shammai asks for a fixed time. any steady pace counts.

practice: Take any book, or a single sheet of paper. Turn one page slowly and listen: the scrape, the small sound as it lands. Read only the first line on the new page, then rest your hand flat on it; that line is enough for today.

wordCard.voice: A page: the daf, one leaf of Talmud with its two sides, read a page a day or a line a day, as long as you keep coming back.

orig.note: Hebrew: a page, a leaf; one leaf of the Talmud has two sides.

carryVoice: Something to keep: any pace counts. A line at a time, little by little, it grows. Catch you tomorrow.
